a moving source has two retarded branches and you do not know which side you are on. What do they leave when they beat against each other?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
definition
beat = ahead - behind

you do not know which side you are on, so both branches are there at half weight each and what you see is the two beating against one another - their difference. The halves cancel out of the difference, which is why the answer does not depend on them being exactly a half but the WAVELENGTH does

definition
ahead = 1 + v

the branch that set out ahead of the source is compressed by its motion - the retarded time carries a 1/(1 - v), which to first order in a small speed is 1 + v

substituting
beat = 1 - behind + v
beat = ahead - behind
ahead = 1 + v
beat = 1 - behind + v

ahead is not a primitive of this theory - it is 1 + v, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

definition
behind = 1 - v

the branch behind is stretched by the same motion by the same amount the other way - 1/(1 + v), which to first order is 1 - v

substituting
beat = 2·v
beat = 1 - behind + v
behind = 1 - v
beat = 2·v

behind is not a primitive of this theory - it is 1 - v, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

two sources are both putting charges into the medium. How often do a charge from each turn up in the same place, r steps out?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4
definition
S = chance · chance'

a meeting needs a charge from EACH source in the same place, so the rate is the chance the first has one there times the chance the second does. Both have travelled and thinned on the way, which is why the rate carries the falloff twice over - and that is what it means for a rate to want two things to coincide

definition
emitted is conserved in flight

what the first source lets go of is carried by transport, which was counted in integers neither making nor unmaking any of what it carries - the same fact that makes deficit conserved, under another name

definition
emitted travels through ρ

what the first source lets go of travels outward through the medium by the same stepping everything else does - it is the same rays

premise
the lattice carries alike in every direction

the exit set's second moment is a multiple of the identity, so nothing carried on this lattice prefers a direction at second order

second moment anisotropy = 0.0000
carrying
emitted goes every way alike

emitteda travels through ρ, and ρ prefers no direction - so neither does what it carries

definition
emitted ∝ m · SHEET

the first source pulses at its own rate - which is what its mass IS here - and each pulse lets go of SHEET charges over its equator. So what it puts into the medium is the one times the other, and SHEET is a count of the tiling rather than anything fitted

spreading
chance ∝ SHEET·mshell

conserved and even, so one site's share is the whole of it over the number of sites there are at that distance

definition
emitted' is conserved in flight

what the second source lets go of is carried by transport, which was counted in integers neither making nor unmaking any of what it carries - the same fact that makes deficit conserved, under another name

definition
emitted' travels through ρ

what the second source lets go of travels outward through the medium by the same stepping everything else does - it is the same rays

carrying
emitted' goes every way alike

emittedb travels through ρ, and ρ prefers no direction - so neither does what it carries

definition
emitted' ∝ m' · SHEET

the second source pulses at its own rate - which is what its mass IS here - and each pulse lets go of SHEET charges over its equator. So what it puts into the medium is the one times the other, and SHEET is a count of the tiling rather than anything fitted

spreading
chance' ∝ SHEET·m'shell

conserved and even, so one site's share is the whole of it over the number of sites there are at that distance

multiplying
S ∝ SHEET2·m·m'shell2

each factor carries its own dependence and they multiply

premise
shell(r) = ball(r) - ball(r-1)

a site is either within r-1 steps or it is not, so the sites at exactly r steps are those within r less those within r-1 - a subtraction, with nothing left over and nothing counted twice

sites within r steps = 8
premise
ball(r) = |r·P ∩ L|
ball(r) = 1, 13, 55, 147, 309, 561, 923, 1415, 2057
Δ1 = 12, 42, 92, 162, 252, 362, 492, 642
Δ2 = 30, 50, 70, 90, 110, 130, 150
Δ3 = 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20

the sites within r steps are the r-fold dilate of the sites within one step - take one step r times and you are somewhere in r·P, and every site of r·P is reached that way. Checked: the counts walked out of the lattice are a polynomial in r of degree 3, which is D, exactly and on integers

sites within r steps = 8; degree of the count in r = 3
Ehrhart's theorem
ball(r) ∝ STEP·rD
ball(r) = |r·P ∩ L|
= β·rD + c1·rD-1 + ... + cD
∝ β·rD

Ehrhart 1962: the number of lattice points in the k-fold dilate of a lattice polytope is a polynomial in k of degree exactly D, whose leading coefficient is the polytope's volume. Here k is r and P is the set of sites one step from the centre, so the ball's count is a polynomial in r of degree D and everything below the leading term is dropped by the proportionality

the difference of a dilate
shell(r) ∝ STEP·rD-1
shell(r) = ball(r) - ball(r-1)
= β·rD - β·(r-1)D
= β·rD - β·(rD - D·rD-1 + ...)
= β·D·rD-1 + ...
∝ β·rD-1

every site is either within r-1 steps or it is not, so the shell is the ball less its own shift by one step. Expanding (r-1)D by the binomial theorem, the leading β·rD cancels against the ball's, and what survives is D·β·rD-1. The D came DOWN from the exponent in that cancellation; a proportionality does not carry it, and the exponent left behind is D-1

expansion
S ∝ SHEET2·m·m'STEP2·r2D-2

shell is not a primitive of this theory - it is what the line above shows it to be, so it stands in for itself here

a meeting needs a charge from EACH source in the same place, so the rate is the chance the first has one there times the chance the second does. Both have travelled and thinned on the way, which is why the rate carries the falloff twice over - and that is what it means for a rate to want two things to coincide

multiplying
S ∝ chance·chance'

each factor carries its own dependence and they multiply

two sources are both putting charges into the medium. How often do a charge from each turn up in the same place, r steps out?
G^XOR^c on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4
definition
S = chance · chance'

a meeting needs a charge from EACH source in the same place, so the rate is the chance the first has one there times the chance the second does. definition
emitted is conserved in flight

what the first source lets go of is carried by transport, which was counted in integers neither making nor unmaking any of what it carries - the same fact that makes deficit conserved, under another name

definition
emitted travels through ρ

what the first source lets go of travels outward through the medium by the same stepping everything else does - it is the same rays

premise
the lattice carries alike in every direction

the exit set's second moment is a multiple of the identity, so nothing carried on this lattice prefers a direction at second order

second moment anisotropy = 0.0000
carrying
emitted goes every way alike

emitteda travels through ρ, and ρ prefers no direction - so neither does what it carries

definition
emitted ∝ m · SHEET

the first source pulses at its own rate - which is what its mass IS here - and each pulse lets go of SHEET charges over its equator. So what it puts into the medium is the one times the other, and SHEET is a count of the tiling rather than anything fitted

spreading
chance ∝ SHEET·mshell

conserved and even, so one site's share is the whole of it over the number of sites there are at that distance

premise
shell(r) = ball(r) - ball(r-1)

a site is either within r-1 steps or it is not, so the sites at exactly r steps are those within r less those within r-1 - a subtraction, with nothing left over and nothing counted twice

sites within r steps = 8
premise
ball(r) = |r·P ∩ L|
ball(r) = 1, 13, 55, 147, 309, 561, 923, 1415, 2057
Δ1 = 12, 42, 92, 162, 252, 362, 492, 642
Δ2 = 30, 50, 70, 90, 110, 130, 150
Δ3 = 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20

the sites within r steps are the r-fold dilate of the sites within one step - take one step r times and you are somewhere in r·P, and every site of r·P is reached that way. Checked: the counts walked out of the lattice are a polynomial in r of degree 3, which is D, exactly and on integers

sites within r steps = 8; degree of the count in r = 3
Ehrhart's theorem
ball(r) ∝ STEP·rD
ball(r) = |r·P ∩ L|
= β·rD + c1·rD-1 + ... + cD
∝ β·rD

Ehrhart 1962: the number of lattice points in the k-fold dilate of a lattice polytope is a polynomial in k of degree exactly D, whose leading coefficient is the polytope's volume. Here k is r and P is the set of sites one step from the centre, so the ball's count is a polynomial in r of degree D and everything below the leading term is dropped by the proportionality

the difference of a dilate
shell(r) ∝ STEP·rD-1
shell(r) = ball(r) - ball(r-1)
= β·rD - β·(r-1)D
= β·rD - β·(rD - D·rD-1 + ...)
= β·D·rD-1 + ...
∝ β·rD-1

every site is either within r-1 steps or it is not, so the shell is the ball less its own shift by one step. Expanding (r-1)D by the binomial theorem, the leading β·rD cancels against the ball's, and what survives is D·β·rD-1. The D came DOWN from the exponent in that cancellation; a proportionality does not carry it, and the exponent left behind is D-1

expansion
S ∝ SHEET2·m·m'STEP2·r2D-2

shell is not a primitive of this theory - it is what the line above shows it to be, so it stands in for itself here

two bodies R apart. Adding the product of what each puts at every point along the line between them, what does it come to - and how does that differ close up?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
definition
met(R) = metfar·(1 + near)

so the whole of it is the long-range law times one plus a correction. The one is what becomes Newton's inverse square; the correction is the middle's logarithm over the long-range term, and it carries c/R - worth per cent at a few cells and nothing at all once R is an astronomical number of lattice steps

definition
metfar = 2 · core

there is a core at each end and they are the same by symmetry. Added to the inverse-square part of the middle, the (R - c) that each carries cancels over a common denominator - which is what makes the long-range law a plain power of R with no trace of the core size left in its exponent

substituting
met(R) = 2·near·core + 2·core
met(R) = metfar + metfar·near
metfar = 2·core
met(R) = 2·near·core + 2·core

metfar is not a primitive of this theory - it is 2·one core, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

definition
near = middlemetfar

the correction is what the middle's tail is worth against the long-range law - a ratio of the two, and the thing that goes to nothing as R grows

definition
middle = ∫Rc tail dx

the middle runs from the edge of one core to the edge of the other, and one over x integrated between them is a logarithm - which grows more slowly than any power, and is the whole of why the correction dies away

definition
tail = R-D·1x

between the two cores the integrand is a genuine product of two falling densities. By partial fractions that splits into a part carrying the same power of the separation as the cores do - which sums with them - and this part, one power of R further down and going as one over the distance along the line. It is the second that gives the correction, and being a power lower is exactly why the correction shrinks as the bodies are moved apart

integrating a power
middle = ln(R/c)RD
middle = ∫Rc 1x dx
= ln(R/c)

the middle's tail goes as one over x, whose integral is a logarithm - so between c and R it is ln(R/c). It grows more slowly than any power of x, which is what matters about it here

one over another
near = 1/2·cD-2·ln(R/c)R
near = middle / metfar
= (ln(R/c)RD) / (2·core)
= 1/2·cD-2·ln(R/c)R

the middle is ln(R/c)RD and metfar is 2·one core, so the one over the other is 1/2·cD-2·ln(R/c)R

substituting
met(R) = 2·core + cD-2·ln(R/c)·coreR
met(R) = 2·near·core + 2·core
near = 1/2·cD-2·ln(R/c)R
met(R) = 2·core + cD-2·ln(R/c)·coreR

near is not a primitive of this theory - it is 1/2·cD-2·ln(R/c)R, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

definition
core = ∫c0 integrand dx

one core runs from the body out to a distance of one core, and across it the integrand is flat - so its contribution is that value times the width

definition
integrand = c-D+1·R-D+1

inside the core at one end the near density has flattened off at its cap - a shell is never smaller than the cell its source sits in - while the far density barely moves across a width of one core. So the integrand there is the product of the two, neither depending on x any more. How fast each thins is the dense regime's: there are partners everywhere, so the hand-off is never what a carrier waits for and the lattice's one-cell-a-tick is the binding bound

integrating a power
core = 1RD-1·cD-2
core = ∫c0 1RD-1·cD-1 dx
= x11, at the limits
= 1RD-1·cD-2

the integrand in a core is 1RD-1·cD-1, a power 0 of x. Integrated that is x1/1, taken between 0 and c

substituting
met(R) = ln(R/c)RD + 2·1RD-1·cD-2
met(R) = 2·core + cD-2·ln(R/c)·coreR
core = 1RD-1·cD-2
met(R) = ln(R/c)RD + 2·1RD-1·cD-2

one core is not a primitive of this theory - it is 1RD-1·cD-2, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

middle = ln(R/c)R(D+1)/2
middle = ∫Rc 1x dx

one over another
near = 1/2·c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)R
near = middle / metfar
= (ln(R/c)R(D+1)/2) / (2·core)
= 1/2·c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)R

the middle is ln(R/c)R(D+1)/2 and metfar is 2·one core, so the one over the other is 1/2·c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)R

substituting
met(R) = 2·core + c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)·coreR
met(R) = 2·near·core + 2·core
near = 1/2·c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)R
met(R) = 2·core + c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)·coreR

near is not a primitive of this theory - it is 1/2·c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)R, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

definition
core = ∫c0 integrand dx

one core runs from the body out to a distance of one core, and across it the integrand is flat - so its contribution is that value times the width

definition
integrand = c(-D+1)/2·R(-D+1)/2

inside the core at one end the near density has flattened off at its cap - a shell is never smaller than the cell its source sits in - while the far density barely moves across a width of one core. So the integrand there is the product of the two, neither depending on x any more. How fast each thins is the thin regime's: partners are scarce, so a carrier waits for one and the hand-off rate is the binding bound - which is what makes the speed follow the density

integrating a power
core = 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2
core = ∫c0 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-1)/2 dx
= x11, at the limits
= 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2

the integrand in a core is 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-1)/2, a power 0 of x. Integrated that is x1/1, taken between 0 and c

substituting
met(R) = ln(R/c)R(D+1)/2 + 2·1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2
met(R) = 2·core + c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)·coreR
core = 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2
met(R) = ln(R/c)R(D+1)/2 + 2·1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2

one core is not a primitive of this theory - it is 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

two bodies R apart. Adding the product of what each puts at every point along the line between them, what does it come to - and how does that differ close up?
G^XOR on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
definition
met(R) = metfar·(1 + near)

so the whole of it is the long-range law times one plus a correction. The one is what becomes Newton's inverse square; the correction is the middle's logarithm over the long-range term, and it carries c/R - worth per cent at a few cells and nothing at all once R is an astronomical number of lattice steps

definition
metfar = 2 · core

there is a core at each end and they are the same by symmetry. Added to the inverse-square part of the middle, the (R - c) that each carries cancels over a common denominator - which is what makes the long-range law a plain power of R with no trace of the core size left in its exponent

substituting
met(R) = 2·near·core + 2·core
met(R) = metfar + metfar·near
metfar = 2·core
met(R) = 2·near·core + 2·core

metfar is not a primitive of this theory - it is 2·one core, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

definition
near = middlemetfar

the correction is what the middle's tail is worth against the long-range law - a ratio of the two, and the thing that goes to nothing as R grows

definition
middle = ∫Rc tail dx

the middle runs from the edge of one core to the edge of the other, and one over x integrated between them is a logarithm - which grows more slowly than any power, and is the whole of why the correction dies away

definition
tail = R-D·1x

between the two cores the integrand is a genuine product of two falling densities. By partial fractions that splits into a part carrying the same power of the separation as the cores do - which sums with them - and this part, one power of R further down and going as one over the distance along the line. It is the second that gives the correction, and being a power lower is exactly why the correction shrinks as the bodies are moved apart

integrating a power
middle = ln(R/c)RD
middle = ∫Rc 1x dx
= ln(R/c)

the middle's tail goes as one over x, whose integral is a logarithm - so between c and R it is ln(R/c). It grows more slowly than any power of x, which is what matters about it here

= (ln(R/c)RD) / (2·core)

the middle is ln(R/c)RD and metfar is 2·one core, so the one over the other is 1/2·cD-2·ln(R/c)R

met(R) = 2·core + c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)·coreR

near is not a primitive of this theory - it is 1/2·c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)R, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

definition
core = ∫c0 integrand dx

one core runs from the body out to a distance of one core, and across it the integrand is flat - so its contribution is that value times the width

definition
integrand = c(-D+1)/2·R(-D+1)/2

inside the core at one end the near density has flattened off at its cap - a shell is never smaller than the cell its source sits in - while the far density barely moves across a width of one core. So the integrand there is the product of the two, neither depending on x any more. How fast each thins is the thin regime's: partners are scarce, so a carrier waits for one and the hand-off rate is the binding bound - which is what makes the speed follow the density

integrating a power
core = 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2
core = ∫c0 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-1)/2 dx
= x11, at the limits
= 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2

the integrand in a core is 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-1)/2, a power 0 of x. Integrated that is x1/1, taken between 0 and c

substituting
met(R) = ln(R/c)R(D+1)/2 + 2·1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2
met(R) = 2·core + c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)·coreR
core = 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2
met(R) = ln(R/c)R(D+1)/2 + 2·1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2

one core is not a primitive of this theory - it is 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

two bodies R apart. Adding the product of what each puts at every point along the line between them, what does it come to - and how does that differ close up?
G^XOR+XOR on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
definition
met(R) = metfar·(1 + near)

so the whole of it is the long-range law times one plus a correction. The one is what becomes Newton's inverse square; the correction is the middle's logarithm over the long-range term, and it carries c/R - worth per cent at a few cells and nothing at all once R is an astronomical number of lattice steps

definition
metfar = 2 · core

there is a core at each end and they are the same by symmetry. Added to the inverse-square part of the middle, the (R - c) that each carries cancels over a common denominator - which is what makes the long-range law a plain power of R with no trace of the core size left in its exponent

substituting
met(R) = 2·near·core + 2·core
met(R) = metfar + metfar·near
metfar = 2·core
met(R) = 2·near·core + 2·core

metfar is not a primitive of this theory - it is 2·one core, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

definition
near = middlemetfar

the correction is what the middle's tail is worth against the long-range law - a ratio of the two, and the thing that goes to nothing as R grows

definition
middle = ∫Rc tail dx

the middle runs from the edge of one core to the edge of the other, and one over x integrated between them is a logarithm - which grows more slowly than any power, and is the whole of why the correction dies away

definition
tail = R-D·1x

between the two cores the integrand is a genuine product of two falling densities. By partial fractions that splits into a part carrying the same power of the separation as the cores do - which sums with them - and this part, one power of R further down and going as one over the distance along the line. It is the second that gives the correction, and being a power lower is exactly why the correction shrinks as the bodies are moved apart

integrating a power
middle = ln(R/c)RD
middle = ∫Rc 1x dx
= ln(R/c)

the middle's tail goes as one over x, whose integral is a logarithm - so between c and R it is ln(R/c). It grows more slowly than any power of x, which is what matters about it here

one over another
near = 1/2·cD-2·ln(R/c)R
near = middle / metfar
= (ln(R/c)RD) / (2·core)
= 1/2·cD-2·ln(R/c)R

the middle is ln(R/c)RD and metfar is 2·one core, so the one over the other is 1/2·cD-2·ln(R/c)R

substituting

inside the core at one end the near density has flattened off at its cap - a shell is never smaller than the cell its source sits in - while the far density barely moves across a width of one core. So the integrand there is the product of the two, neither depending on x any more. How fast each thins is the thin regime's: partners are scarce, so a carrier waits for one and the hand-off rate is the binding bound - which is what makes the speed follow the density

integrating a power
core = 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2
core = ∫c0 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-1)/2 dx
= x11, at the limits
= 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2

the integrand in a core is 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-1)/2, a power 0 of x. Integrated that is x1/1, taken between 0 and c

substituting
met(R) = ln(R/c)R(D+1)/2 + 2·1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2
met(R) = 2·core + c(D-3)/2·ln(R/c)·coreR
core = 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2
met(R) = ln(R/c)R(D+1)/2 + 2·1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2

one core is not a primitive of this theory - it is 1R(D-1)/2·c(D-3)/2, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

how much of the time are two charges opposed, in this theory?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
definition
share = opposedstates

two charges are opposed exactly when their meeting leaves nothing - that is what the word means for a rule that either annihilates a pair or does not. The states a pair can be in are equally available, so how much of the time they are opposed is how many of those states annihilate, over how many there are

premise
opposed = 1

and left nothing at all in the other 1: those are the states in which the two were opposed, which is what being opposed MEANS in a theory whose meetings either annihilate a pair or do not

surviving = 0
premise
states = 1

a ray of G can be carrying nothing but itself, so a facing pair has 1 possible states and the enumeration is complete

cases = 1
a ratio of counts
share = opposedstates = 1
share = opposedstates
= 11
= 1

annihilating is 1 and cases is 1, both counted off the tiling, so the ratio is 1 exactly - and it is worth reading as annihilating/cases rather than as the number, because on another lattice it is a different number and the same ratio

the vacuum makes space wherever it is idle. What does that do to two things sitting some distance apart?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
premise
recession ∝ separation

space is made by idle points splitting, and the only points that can add to the distance between two markers are the ones BETWEEN them - each contributing at most one step when it splits. So how fast they come apart is how many such points there are, times whatever rate each splits at; and the count is proportional to the separation. The rate per point is the vacuum's own business and is not claimed here - what is claimed is that it is the SAME rate everywhere, so the recession goes as the separation with one constant for the whole medium. That is Hubble's law, and it is a count of what lies between rather than a statement about the universe

what is this theory made of - and how many rewrites does making space out of nothing actually take?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
premise
rewrites = 6

G has exactly these 6 rewrites and no others: EMISSION over each Local, gated on "source"; CREATION over each Local; MOVEMENT over the world; ARRIVAL over the world; ANNIHILATION over a chain of Boundary, Boundary, gated on "active"; TRANSPORT over the world. Listed off the theory rather than transcribed, so a theory with a rule taken out reports one fewer without anything here changing

a medium carries something outward from a source. How thick is it at r steps, and does that change when the carriers slow down in thin medium?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
definition
Φ is conserved in flight

the flux is what transport carries, counted where it crosses a shell - so it is conserved for exactly the reason deficit is, which the transport rules were counted doing in integers

definition
Φ = shell · n · v

what crosses a shell in a tick is the number of sites on it, times how much medium is at each, times how fast that medium is moving through. That is what a flux IS, and it mentions no distance

premise
shell(r) = ball(r) - ball(r-1)

a site is either within r-1 steps or it is not, so the sites at exactly r steps are those within r less those within r-1 - a subtraction, with nothing left over and nothing counted twice

sites within r steps = 8
premise
ball(r) = |r·P ∩ L|
ball(r) = 1, 13, 55, 147, 309, 561, 923, 1415, 2057
Δ1 = 12, 42, 92, 162, 252, 362, 492, 642
Δ2 = 30, 50, 70, 90, 110, 130, 150
Δ3 = 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20

the sites within r steps are the r-fold dilate of the sites within one step - take one step r times and you are somewhere in r·P, and every site of r·P is reached that way. Checked: the counts walked out of the lattice are a polynomial in r of degree 3, which is D, exactly and on integers

sites within r steps = 8; degree of the count in r = 3
Ehrhart's theorem
ball(r) ∝ STEP·rD
ball(r) = |r·P ∩ L|
= β·rD + c1·rD-1 + ... + cD
∝ β·rD

Ehrhart 1962: the number of lattice points in the k-fold dilate of a lattice polytope is a polynomial in k of degree exactly D, whose leading coefficient is the polytope's volume. Here k is r and P is the set of sites one step from the centre, so the ball's count is a polynomial in r of degree D and everything below the leading term is dropped by the proportionality

the difference of a dilate
shell(r) ∝ STEP·rD-1
shell(r) = ball(r) - ball(r-1)
= β·rD - β·(r-1)D
= β·rD - β·(rD - D·rD-1 + ...)
= β·D·rD-1 + ...
∝ β·rD-1

every site is either within r-1 steps or it is not, so the shell is the ball less its own shift by one step. Expanding (r-1)D by the binomial theorem, the leading β·rD cancels against the ball's, and what survives is D·β·rD-1. The D came DOWN from the exponent in that cancellation; a proportionality does not carry it, and the exponent left behind is D-1

definition
v ∝ c

a carrier moves at whichever bound is smaller, and in the dense regime that is the lattice's: there are partners everywhere, so the hand-off is never what a carrier waits for and the lattice's one-cell-a-tick is the binding bound. Both bounds were counted off the theory rather than assumed - what is chosen here is only which of them a carrier is waiting on, which is a fact about how thick the medium is at a place

balancing a conserved product
n ∝ 1STEP·rD-1·c
Φ = shell · n · v = constant
STEP·rD-1·c·n = constant
n1 ∝ 1 / (STEP·rD-1·c)
n ∝ 1STEP·rD-1·c

Φ cannot change, and written out it is STEP·rD-1·c·n. n carries the exponent 1 there, so holding the product fixed pins n to the rest raised to -1

a site is either within r-1 steps or it is not, so the sites at exactly r steps are those within r less those within r-1 - a subtraction, with nothing left over and nothing counted twice

sites within r steps = 8
premise
ball(r) = |r·P ∩ L|
ball(r) = 1, 13, 55, 147, 309, 561, 923, 1415, 2057
Δ1 = 12, 42, 92, 162, 252, 362, 492, 642
Δ2 = 30, 50, 70, 90, 110, 130, 150
Δ3 = 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20

the sites within r steps are the r-fold dilate of the sites within one step - take one step r times and you are somewhere in r·P, and every site of r·P is reached that way. Checked: the counts walked out of the lattice are a polynomial in r of degree 3, which is D, exactly and on integers

sites within r steps = 8; degree of the count in r = 3
Ehrhart's theorem
ball(r) ∝ STEP·rD
ball(r) = |r·P ∩ L|
= β·rD + c1·rD-1 + ... + cD
∝ β·rD

Ehrhart 1962: the number of lattice points in the k-fold dilate of a lattice polytope is a polynomial in k of degree exactly D, whose leading coefficient is the polytope's volume. Here k is r and P is the set of sites one step from the centre, so the ball's count is a polynomial in r of degree D and everything below the leading term is dropped by the proportionality

the difference of a dilate
shell(r) ∝ STEP·rD-1
shell(r) = ball(r) - ball(r-1)
= β·rD - β·(r-1)D
= β·rD - β·(rD - D·rD-1 + ...)
= β·D·rD-1 + ...
∝ β·rD-1

every site is either within r-1 steps or it is not, so the shell is the ball less its own shift by one step. Expanding (r-1)D by the binomial theorem, the leading β·rD cancels against the ball's, and what survives is D·β·rD-1. The D came DOWN from the exponent in that cancellation; a proportionality does not carry it, and the exponent left behind is D-1

definition
v ∝ handoff

a carrier moves at whichever bound is smaller, and in the thin regime that is the medium's: partners are scarce, so a carrier waits for one and the hand-off rate is the binding bound - which is what makes the speed follow the density. Both bounds were counted off the theory rather than assumed - what is chosen here is only which of them a carrier is waiting on, which is a fact about how thick the medium is at a place

balancing a conserved product
n ∝ 1STEP1/2·r(D-1)/2·carrier1/2
Φ = shell · n · v = constant
STEP·rD-1·carrier·n2 = constant
n2 ∝ 1 / (STEP·rD-1·carrier)
n ∝ 1STEP1/2·r(D-1)/2·carrier1/2

Φ cannot change, and written out it is STEP·rD-1·carrier·n2. n carries the exponent 2 there - it appears more than once, because the factors are not all independent of it, so holding the product fixed pins n to the rest raised to -1/2

`steer` turns a ray about the field it has accumulated. In a vacuum with nothing driving it, which way does that field point - and what does the answer make the scattering into?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6
definition
\hat{b} = B/|B|

THE AXIS IS NOT A CHOICE, IT IS THE FIELD. `steer` reads `held` - the running sum of polarity times direction over what the ray has met - and turns about THAT, in the sense the charge gives. So the axis is a moment of the same density being steered, which is `vacuum.continuum`'s closure said from the other side

multiplying
\hat{b} ∝ nray

each factor carries its own dependence and they multiply

So the axis is a moment of the same density being steered, which is `vacuum.continuum`'s closure said from the other side

G on fcc-12
premise
g1 = 0.667

<cos gamma> for a turn of THETA about a UNIFORM axis, in closed form: (1 + 2 cos THETA)/3

premise

g1 = 0.3333
a ray is turned a fixed angle about an axis pointing anywhere. Over all the ways the axis could point, how far does the ray actually end up being deflected?
G on square-4, line-2
definition
g1 = (1 + 2\cos\Theta)/3

g1 IS <cos gamma>, AND THE AVERAGE OF t2 OVER A UNIFORM t IS A THIRD. So g1 = cos THETA + (1 - cos THETA)/3 = (1 + 2 cos THETA)/3, with no integral left to do. The higher gl are the same change of variable against Pl and come out of one quadrature - `src/lib/Kernel.ts` does exactly that and agrees with this to 1e-9. Note what it means: at THETA = 120 degrees g1 is nought, and beyond it NEGATIVE - a turn that big is a reversal and undoes a heading rather than nudging it

below the scale where one ray matters, what is left of the rules? Write every one of them as a term in how the density of rays changes, and see what the sum is
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
definition
\nu(1-\rho) = \sigma n\tilde{n} \Rightarrow \rho∞

AND WHAT THE EQUATION IS FOR IS WHAT IT IMPLIES, not the assembling of it. Left alone - no source, nothing streaming in or out, no field to turn about - the transport and the turning both vanish and the line above collapses to what is MADE against what is KILLED. Setting the rate to nought is then a statement about the vacuum on its own: it settles where a neutral point's splitting exactly pays for what the meetings take, nu(1-rho) = sigma·rho2, and that is `vacuum.occupancy`'s own fixed point reached from the continuum side rather than by enumerating the rule

the vacuum splits every neutral point every tick. How fast does empty space actually grow, in this theory?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
definition
expansion = 1

the split fires on a point because the point is NEUTRAL, and it does not ask what this theory's rays carry - so every neutral point makes one point every tick, in every theory here. That is the rate space is made at, and it is the same number whatever is running

which is a number
expansion = 1

1 has nothing left in it that varies, so it is 1 exactly

the vacuum makes space by splitting a point into two halves that meet. How much of what it makes is still there afterwards?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
definition
f = survivingcases

every point the vacuum makes arrives as one facing pair, and the states such a pair can be in are equally available - so how much of what is made is still there is how many states leave something behind, over how many there are

premise
surviving = 0

ANNIHILATION was applied to a real facing pair in each of the 1 states and left something behind in 0 of them: neutral meets neutral: both gone

surviving = 0
premise
cases = 1

a ray of G can be carrying nothing but itself, so a facing pair has 1 possible states and the enumeration is complete

cases = 1
a ratio of counts
f = survivingcases = 0
f = survivingcases
= 01
= 0

surviving is 0 and cases is 1, both counted off the tiling, so the ratio is 0 exactly - and it is worth reading as surviving/cases rather than as the number, because on another lattice it is a different number and the same ratio

surviving = 2
premise
cases = 4

a ray of GXOR can be carrying either sign, so a facing pair has 4 possible states and the enumeration is complete

f = survivingcases = 1/2
f = survivingcases
= 24
= 1/2

surviving is 2 and cases is 4, both counted off the tiling, so the ratio is 1/2 exactly - and it is worth reading as surviving/cases rather than as the number, because on another lattice it is a different number and the same ratio

f = survivingcases

every point the vacuum makes arrives as one facing pair, and the states such a pair can be in are equally available - so how much of what is made is still there is how many states leave something behind, over how many there are

premise
surviving = 2

ANNIHILATION was applied to a real facing pair in each of the 4 states and left something behind in 2 of them: -1 meets -1: both still there; -1 meets 1: both gone; 1 meets -1: both gone; 1 meets 1: both still there

surviving = 2
premise
cases = 4

a ray of GXORc can be carrying either sign, so a facing pair has 4 possible states and the enumeration is complete

cases = 4
a ratio of counts
f = survivingcases = 1/2
f = survivingcases
= 24
= 1/2

surviving is 2 and cases is 4, both counted off the tiling, so the ratio is 1/2 exactly - and it is worth reading as surviving/cases rather than as the number, because on another lattice it is a different number and the same ratio

the vacuum makes space by splitting a point into two halves that meet. How much of what it makes is still there afterwards?

the continuum model has an absorption and a scattering in it. What sets the two, and how much freedom is actually left once the rules have spoken?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
definition
\sigmas = \sigmaa = 1

AND `steer` SPENDS ONE RING STEP PER TICK, so stir is 1 per tick too, and absorb = stir IDENTICALLY. A ray is exactly as likely to be destroyed as turned. That is not a regime that was chosen, it is where the rules put themselves, and it matters for how the model must be solved: with scattering and absorption comparable the medium is NEARLY BALLISTIC, most of what arrives anywhere arrived straight, and a moment expansion of the direction - PL - cannot represent that at any usable order. Measured, such a solve moved 45% between L = 9 and L = 15 and missed the exact ballistic profile by a factor of thirty

definition
\sigmaa = \sigma·\rho∞ = (1/\rho∞)·\rho∞ = 1

AND THE TWO CANCEL. The cross-section read off the rule is 1/occ and the vacuum settles AT occ - the same number, because it is the same balance seen twice - so the annihilation rate is 1 per tick ON EVERY LATTICE. The occupancies differ by 68% between fcc-12 and icosahedral-12 and this does not move at all, which is the sort of thing that is either a coincidence or the point

a number is an expression
\sigmaa = 1

\sigmaa is 1, so it can stand in an expression as that

substituting
\sigmas = 1
\sigmas = \sigmaa
\sigmaa = 1
\sigmas = 1

\sigmaa is not a primitive of this theory - it is 1, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

which is a number
\sigmas = 1

1 has nothing left in it that varies, so it is 1 exactly

a body's cells belong to a source, so the split does not fire on them. What does that do to the expansion around it - and is that gravity?
G on fcc-12, cubic-6, square-4, line-2
definition
deficit = A' · expansion

each blocked cell is one point that would have expanded and did not, so the shortfall is how many are blocked times how fast each would have grown. THIS IS GRAVITY IN THIS MODEL: not a pull between bodies but an expansion that did not happen, spreading outward from whatever was in the way. A second body is pushed toward it because fewer rays arrive from that direction than from the far side

definition
A' = A'

the split fails to fire at every cell the body owns, so the suppression itself goes as its volume - but a shortfall deep inside is filled in by its neighbours before it gets out. What reaches the medium beyond has to cross the boundary, and how many ways there are through it is the body's area. So what a distant body feels is limited by the surface, and a bigger surface pulls harder

substituting
deficit = A'·expansion
deficit = A'·expansion
A' = A'
deficit = A'·expansion

blocked is not a primitive of this theory - it is A', so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out

cited
expansion = 1

established earlier by vacuum.expansion, on this same theory and lattice - the working is there rather than repeated here

a number is an expression
expansion = 1

expansion is 1, so it can stand in an expression as that

substituting
deficit = A'
deficit = A'·expansion
expansion = 1
deficit = A'

expansion is not a primitive of this theory - it is 1, so it stands in for itself here and the result is multiplied out
